memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "If an animal that you are allowed to eat dies, anyone who touches its carcass will be unclean till evening. Anyone who eats some of it must wash their clothes, and they will be unclean till evening. Anyone who picks up the carcass must wash their clothes, and they will be unclean till evening." - Lev 11:39-40 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Here is a detail easily missed. Even a clean animal — a permitted one, perfectly acceptable at the table — brings uncleanness once it has died on its own.

The issue is no longer the species. It is death itself.

That is the heartbeat running through this whole chapter. Death was not part of God's good creation. It entered through sin (Rom 5:12), and it does not belong. So in Israel's daily life, God attached a visible reminder to it: wherever death is found, something is not right. Wash. Wait. Remember.

Our culture has a hundred ways of dressing death up — calling it natural, or a circle, or simply the way things are. Scripture will not do that. Paul calls it the last enemy (1 Cor 15:26). An enemy is something to be defeated, not accepted.

And that is exactly what Christ has done. He entered death, and it could not hold Him. The stone rolled away. The One who touched the dead and made them live has emptied the grave of its final word.

For the believer, death remains an enemy — but a defeated one. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? (1 Cor 15:55).

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. How do you usually think and speak about death?
2. What difference does Christ's resurrection make to your fear of it?
3. Who around you needs the hope of the empty tomb today?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord Jesus, thank You that You faced death and defeated it. When I grieve or fear, anchor me in the certainty of Your resurrection and the hope of my own. Amen.
